One explanation, from Harvard astronomer Avi Loeb, suggests that 1998 KY26 is a derelict Soviet spacecraft that launched almost 40 years ago. More conventional attempts to account for its acceleration proffer that it’s a “dark comet,” a type of space object that acts like a rocky asteroid, but experiences acceleration that can’t be accounted for by gravitational forces. Yet according to new research published in the journal Icarus , it’s too warm to be a dark comet, which can accelerate by releasing ice that sublimates into gas. If that were the case, observations show that it would’ve run out of ice reserves a long time ago. “Our temperature model results indicate that the water outgassing rate on 1998 KY26 would be too high to maintain buried ice, refining the understanding of the asteroid’s composition,” authors of the paper and Georgia Institute of Technology aerospace engineers Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi wrote. 1998 KY26 is a 36-foot space object that rotates every five and a half minutes and is currently located 186 million miles away from Earth. After modeling its temperature using pre-existing data, Hansen and Hirabayashi found that even its coldest regions measured upwards of -77 degrees Fahrenheit. candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX will make spaceflight history this week, if all goes according to plan. The company announced over the weekend that it's targeting Friday (Nov. 13) for the 15th test flight of its Starship megarocket, which will attempt something that's never been done before. "The upcoming flight is planned to be the first to return both Starship and Super Heavy to the launch site for catch," SpaceX wrote in a description of Flight 15 . "If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket." SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 14th test flight on Sept. 28, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Super Heavy is Starship's giant booster, and Starship (or Ship for short) is its upper-stage spacecraft. candidates.title: RFA Confirms Inaugural RFA ONE Launch Has Slipped to 2027
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: RFA German launch company Rocket Factory Augsburg (RFA) has confirmed that it is now targeting 2027 for the inaugural flight of its RFA ONE rocket from a Scottish launch facility. The revised target for the rocket’s inaugural flight was announced in a post published on the company’s LinkedIn page on 3 November. The post detailed a visit from Walther Pelzer, Director General of the German Space Agency at DLR. “We discussed what it takes to turn RFA into a global launch service provider,” the 3 November post explained. “In doing so, we received invaluable input, along with a clear expectation for 2027, one we fully share: the successful first flight of RFA ONE, the objective we’re now rallying behind on our #RoadtoLaunch.” The statement marks the first time RFA has publicly acknowledged a 2027 launch target since the rocket planned for the flight was destacked for an investigation. The company has not yet provided a more specific launch window. RFA announced in March that it had delivered the first and second stages of RFA ONE to SaxaVord in Scotland, with an inaugural flight planned for the summer. The vehicle was subsequently fully integrated and stacked on the launch pad in July ahead of a planned first-stage static fire test. On 28 July, RFA announced that it had encountered an issue during testing that required the vehicle to be de-stacked for further investigation and potential corrective action. The company did not disclose the nature of the issue at the time. The setback did, however, result in the cancellation of a five-week launch window scheduled to open on 10 August. During an earnings call on 6 August, Marco Fuchs, CEO of RFA’s majority shareholder OHB, which holds a 65.1% stake in the launch company, stated that “the first test flight is still planned for later this year.” Fuchs explained that the rocket had been returned to the integration hall to allow engineers to re-examine its tanks, adding that it would be re-erected on the launch pad soon.

candidates.title: COP31 in Türkiye: Can the world turn climate pledges into action?
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The 31st session of the Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) is set to begin on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, running through November 20.

The summit faces a central challenge: turning national pledges into measurable emissions cuts and stronger support for vulnerable countries.

Implementation is a key focus of the Turkish COP31 presidency.

Its 2035 targets include raising share of final energy demand met by electricity from just over 20% today to 35%, and reducing energy consumption intensity in the building sector by at least 25%.

The presidency is also seeking to advance zero waste, methane reduction, food security and green industrialization.

A major test will be whether countries can close the gap between their national climate plans and the goals of the Paris Agreement.

A synthesis report released by the UNFCCC Secretariat on October 27 recorded 127 new nationally determined contributions (NDCs), representing 154 parties to the Paris Agreement, submitted between January 2024 and August 2026.

Together, they cover about 71% of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2019, excluding land use, land-use change and forestry.

China successfully launched the 29th group of satellites for its low-Earth-orbit satellite internet constellation from the Hainan commercial space launch site in Wenchang, south China's Hainan Province, on Monday.

A Long March-12 carrier rocket blasted off at 4:24 a.m., sending the satellites into their preset orbit.

The Long March-12, measuring about 62 meters in length, is a new-generation Chinese launch vehicle that uses cryogenic liquid propellants. It is the country's first single-core rocket with a diameter in the 4-meter class. The rocket has a payload capacity of at least 6 tonnes to a sun-synchronous orbit at an altitude of 700 kilometers and can support both single-satellite and multi-satellite launches into different orbits.

The launch marked the 676th flight mission of the Long March carrier rocket series.

candidates.title: Climate Change Has Become So Bad That Rice Krispies Don’t Have Actual Rice in Them Anymore
candidates.raw_excerpt: Snap, Crackle, and Pop! The sonic slogan of Rice Krispies is now becoming an anachronism. The classic puffed rice foodstuff now no longer contain actual rice grains, at least in UK and European markets, the manufacturer Kellogg’s recently admitted . It will now use rice flour and corn flour, which aside from gustatory concerns, will result in it being noticeably quieter than it used to be. Kellogg’s, in the face of complaints online, insists that retaining the original sound was a “huge focus.” It’s yet another example of the corporate cost-cutting putrefaction we’ve come to expect — and the reason for it is grim: climate change. A spokesperson told media outlets that the reformulation will help “maintain consistent quality at a time when changing weather conditions are affecting the quality and availability of some of the rice and grains used in our cereals.” The company didn’t get into specifics, but the recipe change comes as a powerful “ super El Niño ” climate phenomenon has devastated agriculture in South and Southeast Asia , where more than half the world’s rice is grown. Scientists say that the impacts of the weather event, which is on track to be the most powerful of its kind in recorded history, has been exacerbated by climate change. The “changing weather patterns” referred to by the Kellogg’s spokesperson was an understatement. El Niño is characterized by warming ocean surface temperatures in the Pacific. This kicks off a chain reaction that causes formidable storms and rainfall in the Americas while severely disrupting rainfall patterns and bringing devastating droughts across Asia. candidates.raw_excerpt: One key debate still swirling around men’s health: is it better to pee standing, or sitting down? It may seem like a silly question, but there is some scientific merit to the question. Previous studies have found that men with prostate issues or urinary complications could be better off sitting, pointing to the possibility that plopping down may help loosen up pelvic floor muscles. Unfortunately, the evidence available is far from conclusive — which is probably what inspired the Colombian Urology Research Group to plow ahead with a new study published in the journal Neurourology and Urodynamics . The research, first flagged by Science Alert , took a look at the “posture adopted during voiding” of 52 male volunteers, 24 of whom stood while the rest sat. Each group went on a 24 hour “washout” break in between tests. During the examination, researchers looked at maximum urine flow rate, as well as the total volume of urine expelled in one go. Despite previous polarizing studies on the topic, this piece of research yielded a dull conclusion: it just doesn’t seem to matter. “In healthy men, voiding posture did not significantly modify the maximum urinary flow rate or voided volume,” the team wrote. The one difference between the two postures, the scientists noted, was in what might be called “acceleration.” “The sitting position was associated with a shorter time to maximum flow,” the scientists wrote, noting that it’s a “small difference that is unlikely to be clinically meaningful and was partly dependent on a single outlier.” Still, you never know until you try.
